  relationship_status: Single

  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Arthur had come to believe that the basement evening ten years ago had permanently altered how he navigated his own life. The memory did not arrive as a linear story but as a set of sharp, inescapable fragments. He knew the exact weight of two men pinning his arms to the floor, knew the frayed wool of one man’s sleeve against his cheek, knew the cold slick of sweat and the complete inability of his own legs to push back. The details remained painfully clear, yet when he tried to hold the full event in his mind, sections simply vanished, leaving him with a wordless certainty that he had been completely overpowered. He could name what happened, but he could not find the words to describe it, as though language had been stripped away along with his agency. What frightened him most was the realization that his own body had not reacted the way he expected, as though it could no longer be trusted to signal danger or protect him from it. In the years since, his days have narrowed into a careful routine. Arthur avoids new neighborhoods and unfamiliar coffee shops, not out of disinterest, but since he cannot reliably assess the people inside or map the exits. When he steps outside, his attention locks onto the spaces around him. He watches men’s hands, their shoulders, the way they stand in doorways, searching for any flicker of intention that might signal another loss of control. His tutoring sessions in the community center’s glass-walled room have become the stage for his most acute struggles. He always arrives early and claims a desk against the far wall, insisting on a chair that lets him see the entire room. He tells himself this is merely practical, but it is really about survival. When students begin to arrive, Arthur keeps his posture rigid. He refuses to sit within reaching distance of any man, and when a learner once asked him to reorganize the shared study table, Arthur felt his jaw tighten, certain that another person taking control of his space was just another step toward being forced to do something. If a student approaches too closely or places a hand on his shoulder to point at a textbook, Arthur will suddenly stand, gather his papers, and retreat to the stairwell. He lights a cigarette there not for the taste, but for the deliberate pause it forces into his day. He has learned to step away from conversations that grow intense or personal, shutting his face down whenever his pulse quickens, because letting himself feel the full weight of what is happening feels like opening a door to that basement again. The distance between him and other people has become a quiet architecture. Friends have stopped calling, and Arthur no longer minds the silence, though he feels the isolation like a physical weight. He works steadily enough, moving from student to student with careful, measured instructions, but the work has lost its former spontaneity. What finally brought him to his current appointment was a session last week when a former student, now in his late twenties, had reached across the desk to grip Arthur’s wrist, insisting Arthur look at a particular equation. Arthur’s breath had stopped, his chest had locked, and he had stumbled backward, knocking over his water bottle. He had walked out of the building, smoked three cigarettes in his car, and sat there until the engine cooled, certain that he was losing the ability to function at all. He was not sure what he expected from the therapist, only that he needed someone who could help him stop flinching at the sound of his own door closing, and maybe, eventually, learn how to trust his own hands again.
